prompt: Some people think students should be allowed to use calculators in all math classes. Write an essay arguing for or against this.
text:
# Calculators Belong in Some Math Classes, Not All

Calculators are useful tools, and students should learn to use them well. But allowing them in every math class, at every level, would be a mistake. Some classes exist to build skills that a calculator would replace, and students need those skills before they can use the tool wisely.

The strongest argument for calculators is that they free students to think. In a statistics or calculus class, the hard part is understanding the idea, not grinding through arithmetic. A student who spends ten minutes finding a square root by hand may lose track of what the problem was asking. Calculators also mirror the real world. Engineers, nurses, and accountants all use them, so learning the tool is practical preparation.

However, this argument only works for students who already understand the basics. In early math classes, the arithmetic is the lesson. A child learning multiplication is not just trying to get an answer. She is learning how numbers relate to each other. If she types every problem into a device, she may never notice that 6 × 7 is the same as 7 × 6, or that multiplying by 10 shifts the digits. These patterns become the foundation for algebra later. Students who skip them often struggle when the symbols get more abstract.

Number sense is another reason to limit calculators. A student with good number sense can look at an answer and tell whether it is reasonable. If she accidentally types 4,000 instead of 400, she will notice that her result is far too large. A student who has always relied on the device has no such check. She will trust whatever appears on the screen. Calculators do exactly what they are told, including when the instructions are wrong.

Fairness also matters. If every class allows calculators at all times, teachers lose the ability to test whether students understand a method. A correct answer on the screen does not show that the student knows why it is correct. Teachers need some assignments and tests where the thinking, not the button pressing, is what gets measured.

A better approach is to match the tool to the goal. Early grades should focus on mental math and written methods. Middle grades can introduce calculators gradually, alongside lessons on estimating answers. In high school and beyond, calculators can be standard equipment, since students have the foundation to use them well.

In short, calculators should serve understanding, not replace it. Letting students use them in all math classes would weaken the very skills that make calculators useful. Allowing them when students are ready, and withholding them when the skill itself is the lesson, gives students the best of both.
